title: Big Ten expands replay review audio to all conference games starting September 12
dek: The Big Ten announced Wednesday it will broadcast live audio between game referees and replay officials during all conference football games and home non-conference matchups officiated by Big Ten officials, effective September 12. The move follows a controversial clock discrepancy in last weekend's Michigan-Western Michigan game that allowed the Wolverines an extra second to score a winning touchdown.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Live replay review audio and Replay Center video feeds will be available to all Big Ten conference and home non-conference broadcasts beginning Saturday, September 12, addressing transparency concerns after the Michigan-Western Michigan finish.
bottom_line: The Big Ten's September 12 rollout will test whether making replay review audio and Replay Center footage visible to broadcasters and viewers prevents future clock disputes or only makes the disagreement between officials and stadium operators visible in real time. Whether the NCAA's new embedded clock standard actually prevents similar discrepancies during future high-stakes moments will emerge only after the protocol faces its first critical decision.
body: The Big Ten announced Wednesday it will expand live audio broadcasts of replay reviews to all conference football games and home non-conference matchups officiated by Big Ten officials, beginning Saturday, September 12.

The announcement follows a highly controversial finish to last Saturday's Michigan-Western Michigan game, when officials granted the Wolverines an extra second after the game clock struck zero, allowing a Hail Mary touchdown pass to win the game. According to Awful Announcing's reporting, officials cited a discrepancy between the clock they were using and the stadium and broadcast clocks as the reason for what became known as the phantom second.

Prior to this expansion, the Big Ten had announced it would provide live audio between the game referee and replay official during reviews, along with a live shot from inside the Big Ten Replay Center, but only for Friday night games. Beginning September 12, all football broadcasts from Big Ten venues that include Big Ten replay and on-field officials will be able to feature live audio between the game referee and replay official during reviews, alongside video of the game footage being viewed during the process and a view inside the Big Ten Replay Center, per the reporting.

The expanded transparency initiative aligns with broader conference moves in college football. The ACC completed its first full season providing networks with similar replay review insights in 2025, and the Big 12 is rolling out similar replay review access this season.

The NCAA has also moved to standardize clock procedures following the Michigan-Western Michigan incident. According to ESPN's reporting on an internal NCAA memo, the official time for any game is the time displayed on the in-stadium game clock, but when a replay review requires time to be restored, the replay official's decision must be based on the embedded game clock contained within the broadcast's program feed, or the game-clock graphic if no embedded clock is available. The NCAA rule represents a shift from relying solely on the stadium clock to incorporating broadcast clock feeds as a backup standard.
